newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Hugo Boss breaks into women's range.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Hugo Boss breaks into women's range.

text.p: Germany's Hugo Boss AG on Monday revealed plans to launch its first women's fashion range while forecasting moderate sales and profit growth this year after a strong 1996.

The German clothes retailer which made its name with trend-setting menswear will next year break with tradition with a range aimed at the "avant garde" women who are already buying men's items from Boss's top fashion Hugo label for themselves.

Boss, which is majority-owned by Italy's Marzotto Group MTZI.MI, said the launch of Hugo Woman, along with plans for a golf-wear range, seen generating 50 million marks ($30 million) in yearly sales, was part of its strategy to focus on the top end of the market.
"We don't see our future in reducing our prices. We see our future as a strong international brand," chairman Joachim Vogt told a news conference.
"We have done a great deal to strengthen and expand our key brand Boss in a difficult environment. I am sure we can achieve this with the team we have built up," Vogt said.

Boss has seen strong growth in the past four years from its decision to split its product lines into three groups from one -- Boss for traditional buyers, Hugo for younger more adventurous buyers and Baldessarini for top-line customers.

But the company has been hampered by boardroom problems after Boss chief executive Peter Littmann, 49, left the firm at the start of 1997 after an apparent dispute with Marzotto officials over the direction of the Stuttgart- based group.
Vogt, a 44-year-old production and logistics executive at Boss, said he was confident of success in his new post.

Brushing aside suggestions that Boss could lose autonomy under Marzotto's control, Vogt said: "Our experiences with Marzotto have been very good so far. They leave us on a very long line and I see absolutely no reason why that should change."

Vogt forecast a five percent rise in both sales and earnings for 1997, with sales expected to reach 1.05 billion marks, topping last year's record 995.3 million marks, and net income to rise to 68.5 million marks from 64.9 million.

Boss's reported net profit figure for 1996 was 76.1 million marks, but that included a one-off tax benefit associated with its special bonus dividend payout of 57 marks per share and is therefore not an accurate comparison.
Discounting the dividend effect, earnings rose 11 percent in 1996 and sales rose 10.5 percent.
The group said that sales rose significantly in the first three months of the current year, but said this could not be extrapolated for the full year because of seasonal fluctuations.

Vogt acknowledged that difficult economic conditions in many industrialised countries were hampering sales but said Boss was pinning its hope for growth on developing markets, epecially Southeast Asia and eastern Europe.
Boss shops, which sell the conservative Boss label clothes which still account for the vast bulk of the company's sales, are to appear as early as possible in all eastern European cities, Vogt said.
The company is also keen on expanding in Britain and Spain and is to open a flagship store in Los Angeles later this year.
Turning to the Hugo Woman range, Vogt said a limited collection would be in the shops from next Autumn and would be expanded to a full range over time.
But he was vague on the sales forecasts for the new line, saying only that the women's line should match sales of the Hugo men's line within five years.
Hugo label sales were 41.1 million marks last year and are expected to rise about 15 percent in 1997.
"We are optimistic for the women's line but it is also a new field for us," Vogt said. $ = 1.685 German Marks)
